Title: #NSTviral: SUV driver criticised after tailgating ambulance
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: An SUV driver has drawn widespread criticism after being seen tailgating an ambulance, prompting calls for action by the Road Transport Department.
In the
55-second video filmed by a passenger in the ambulance,
the SUV driver was seen taking advantage of the path cleared by motorists who had moved to the side to let the emergency vehicle pass.
The driver also had the vehicle's hazard lights switched on while closely following the ambulance.
The video was uploaded to the "DashCam Owners Malaysia" Facebook page on July 30 by user Muhammhd Alif Danial.
Alif urged the online community to lodge official complaints against the driver.
The video quickly drew criticism from social media users, many of whom demanded severe penalties to deter other motorists from engaging in similar practices.
Facebook user Howseng Lee called for the driver's driving privileges to be revoked.
"Revoke their licence immediately so that people like this will be afraid to do something like this in the future," he commented.
Another user, Chek Fizie, tagged the authorities in the comments and said: "Road Transport Department, please revoke their licence."
Meanwhile, commenter Khairul Afqar Yusof reminded the poster that specific details were needed for the authorities to act on the submission.
"Provide the details of the time and location. To report to the Road Transport Department, you need this information," he said

Title: No distance too great: Woman returns home to vote
Article:
JELEBU: For Lim Qui Fah, no distance was too great to exercise her democratic right.
The 67-year-old flew home from Australia specifically to cast her ballot in the Negri Sembilan election for the Chennah state seat.
She arrived in Malaysia yesterday and was the first voter in line at SJK(C) Chun Yin in Titi at 7.40am today, ahead of the polling centre opening at 8am.
Speaking to reporters, Lim said returning to vote was a responsibility she could not ignore.
"It is very important for my country. It is my responsibility, so I had to come back to fulfil it. I believe I can do it. Malaysia Boleh," she said, adding that she has never missed an election.
Although she now lives in Australia, Lim said Chennah remains her hometown.
She said she was determined to return to fulfil her civic duty, describing voting as a responsibility she has never taken lightly.
The Chennah seat is witnessing a straight fight between Pakatan Harapan's Anthony Loke and Barisan Nasional's Siow Kong Choon.
Loke, who is Transport Minister and DAP secretary-general, has held the seat since 2013.
In the 2023 state election, he retained it with a majority of more than 2,200 votes.
Chennah is one of Negri Sembilan's most balanced state seats, with Malays making up about 46 per cent of the electorate and Chinese voters accounting for 44 per cent.

Title: 'I always feared this day would come,' says husband
Article:
KUALA NERUS: A man whose pregnant wife and teenage son were injured in a crash involving a motorcyclist believed to be attending the RXZ Members 8.0 gathering said he had always feared for her safety whenever she left home.
Talhah Mahmud, 61, said his wife, Syafirah Salim, 36, who is seven months pregnant with their third child, and their eldest son, Ahmad Asyraf, 13, were on their way from their home in Kampung Tanjung Sabtu to Batu Enam market to buy daily necessities when the crash occurred at the Jalan Buluh Gading four-way junction at 11.50am yesterday.
"Whenever my heavily pregnant wife went out, I could never shake the feeling that something might happen. I never imagined she and our eldest son would be involved in an accident.
"I was also injured in a motorcycle accident about five months ago after hitting a cat while riding home from the mosque. I fractured my knee and am still undergoing physiotherapy. I now walk with the aid of a stick and spend most of my time at home," he said when contacted.
Talhah said he was informed that another motorcycle had collided with the Honda Beat ridden by his wife, causing both motorcycles to catch fire.
"I was told my son suffered burns to about 60 per cent of his body, from the waist down. He is now at Hospital Sultanah Nur Zahirah in Kuala Terengganu and is due to undergo surgery," he said.
Talhah admitted he could not bring himself to watch the viral video of the crash involving his wife and son.
He prayed for their swift recovery and hoped the unborn baby had not been affected.
"I do not blame anyone. I accept what has happened and leave the matter to the authorities to investigate," he said.
Earlier, it was reported that the motorcycle carrying the mother and son collided with another motorcycle believed to have been ridden by a participant of the RXZ Members 8.0 gathering.
The crash left Syafirah's motorcycle completely destroyed by fire, while the other motorcycle was about 80 per cent burnt. Its rider reportedly suffered hand injuries.

Title: Spain says almost all migrants have returned to Morocco from Ceuta
Article:
MADRID, (Spain): Almost all of the migrants who entered Ceuta have returned to Morocco, the Spanish foreign minister announced Friday, saying "enough of the deliberate misinformation."
"It is not possible to travel from Ceuta and Melilla to mainland Spain without identifying yourself at a police checkpoint," Jose Manuel Albares wrote on X, according to Anadolu Ajansi.
"The integrity of the Schengen Area is fully guaranteed. Enough of the deliberate misinformation."
Spanish news agency EFE reported earlier that hundreds of migrants were heading toward the border Friday afternoon to return to Morocco, citing a repatriation agreement between Spain and Morocco as well as the lack of open shops, supermarkets and restaurants in Ceuta to meet basic needs.
Spain's Civil Guard and the Army's Regulares Group No. 54 were deployed along Tarajal beach area to prevent further arrivals by sea.
According to Spanish authorities, at least 57 people have died in the migration crisis.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday described the mass arrival of migrants into Ceuta since Thursday as "an attack" and "a violation of Spain's territorial integrity," pledging to restore normality "as soon as possible." — BERNAMA

Title: MBSB commits RM4bil to Malaysia's high-growth industries
Article:
PETALING JAYA: MBSB Bank is ramping up its support for Malaysia's high-growth, high-value (HGHV) industries, committing RM4 billion across four strategic sectors as it positions itself to play a larger role in financing the country's industrial transformation.
The bank has earmarked RM1 billion each for the rail, aerospace, automotive and renewable energy sectors, while mobilising more than RM4.7 billion in sustainable and transition financing to date.
MBSB group chairman Datuk Wan Kamaruzaman Wan Ahmad said demand for financing under the bank's HGHV initiative has met expectations, with the lender prepared to increase its allocation if the pipeline of quality projects continues to grow.
"We are prepared to consider a larger allocation if demand continues to grow and proposals meet the required financing and eligibility criteria," he told Business Times on the sidelines of the TechnoMART Malaysia: High Tech Financing 2026 event.
The financing initiative is part of MBSB's strategy to diversify beyond its traditional strength in property financing by supporting companies operating in advanced manufacturing and technology-driven industries.
Kamaruzaman said the bank's financing focus extends beyond the four priority sectors to companies involved in electrical and electronics, semiconductors, digital technology, artificial intelligence and green technology.
Financing is available for machinery and equipment purchases, working capital, capacity expansion and technology commercialisation, helping businesses move from research and development into commercial production.
He said the strategy is aligned with the government's aspirations under the 13th Malaysia Plan and the New Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030, both of which aim to strengthen domestic industrial capabilities, encourage technology adoption and improve access to financing for innovation.
"Our priority is to provide practical financing that helps Malaysian companies invest, scale and compete in the industries shaping the country's next phase of growth," he said.
To support these ambitions, MBSB has established partnerships across key industries.
In the rail sector, the bank has allocated up to RM1 billion through its collaboration with the Malaysia Rail Industry Corporation to support small and medium enterprises, technology providers and solution developers.
For renewable energy, another RM1 billion has been set aside to finance solar projects and accelerate Malaysia's clean energy transition.
The bank has also partnered with Weststar Group, providing RM1.3 billion in financing to support the company's aviation expansion plans.
More recently, MBSB signed a memorandum of understanding with the Northern Corridor Implementation Authority (NCIA), backed by a RM1 billion financing line for eligible businesses, investors and strategic projects across the Northern Corridor Economic Region (NCER).
The financing will help companies establish new operations, expand production capacity and participate in larger domestic and regional supply chains.
Kamaruzaman said MBSB is working closely with industry bodies and development agencies to better understand sector-specific financing needs and identify credible investment opportunities.
He said many high-technology companies require significant capital for specialised machinery, automation, commercialisation and business expansion, creating opportunities for banks to play a more active role in supporting industrial development.
MBSB is also leveraging its subsidiary, Malaysian Industrial Development Finance Bhd (MIDF), to create a more integrated financing ecosystem.
MIDF continues to administer government-backed financing schemes, including the Soft Financing Scheme for Automation and Modernisation and the Soft Financing Scheme for Digital and Technology.
Meanwhile, MBSB Bank complements these offerings through Shariah-compliant commercial financing, transaction banking and deposit solutions, allowing companies to continue their banking relationship as they grow beyond the development stage.
Kamaruzaman said businesses receiving development financing through MIDF can also channel their funds into MBSB Bank accounts to manage operating cash flow, payments and deposits within the same group.
Speaking at the event, Kamaruzaman said Malaysia must continue investing in innovation despite growing global uncertainties driven by geopolitical tensions, fragmented trade policies and rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI).
He noted that AI is becoming one of the world's defining technologies, with global investment expected to reach US$2.53 trillion this year.
He also pointed to the strong debut of integrated circuit design company SkyeChip, whose initial public offering gained more than 150 per cent from its offer price after being oversubscribed 95 times.
However, he stressed that many promising technologies fail to reach commercialisation because of limited access to financing and industry support.
"Many technologies developed work perfectly in the laboratory and still never reach the market. Not because the innovation was wrong, but because of the lack of infrastructure to turn it into a business.
"That gap does not close on the strength of better ideas. It closes with capital, partnerships, and with institutions willing to understand what a technology company needs," he said.
Kamaruzaman said initiatives such as TechnoMART Malaysia provide an important platform to connect innovators, investors, financial institutions and government agencies.
He said this helps accelerate commercialisation and attract greater private sector investment into Malaysia's technology ecosystem.
He added that backing innovation is ultimately about supporting Malaysia's long-term economic growth, with stronger local companies expected to play a larger role in global supply chains as the country advances towards a high-income, innovation-driven economy.

Title: N9 polls: All 401 polling centres opened at 8am
Article:
SEREMBAN: A total of 401 polling centres involving 1,668 streams for the 16th Negri Sembilan state election opened simultaneously at 8am today, with 859,760 registered voters, including 7,391 postal voters, eligible to cast their ballots for the 36 state seats.
Voting will continue until 6pm at polling centres located at schools, community halls, public halls and colleges.
The Election Commission (EC) is targeting a voter turnout of between 72 and 75 per cent, with initial results expected as early as 10pm and the full results before midnight.
A total of 14,995 early voters, or 91.06 per cent, cast their ballots on July 28, surpassing the EC's target of 90 per cent.
Meanwhile, Bernama checks at several locations found weather conditions to be generally fine this morning.
According to the Malaysian Meteorological Department, most areas in the seven districts of Seremban, Jempol, Jelebu, Kuala Pilah, Tampin, Port Dickson and Rembau are expected to remain clear until noon.
However, heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast in most parts of the state in the afternoon.
The 16th Negri Sembilan state election sees 103 candidates, with Pakatan Harapan (PH) contesting all 36 seats, followed by Barisan Nasional (BN) with 25, Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) with 24, Perikatan Nasional (PN) with 11 and four independent candidates.
Barisan Jamaah Islamiah Se-Malaysia (Berjasa), Parti Orang Asli Malaysia (ASLI) and Parti Sosialis Malaysia (PSM) are each fielding one candidate.
For the latest updates on the 16th Negri Sembilan state election, visit [https://prn.bernama.com/n9](https://prn.bernama.com/n9).

Title: Govt wants EV charging network to keep pace with adoption [WATCH]
Article:
TANJUNG MALIM: Malaysia must accelerate the rollout of electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure while ensuring foreign automakers help develop the country's automotive ecosystem, the Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry said.
Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said his ministry will work with Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) and other stakeholders to strengthen the country's EV charging network as adoption gathers pace.
Johari said the ministry is targeting 30,000 public EV chargers nationwide, although no timeline has been set. Malaysia currently has about 1,000 public charging stations.
He added that the government had forgone RM3.3 billion in tax revenue over the past four years by exempting imported EVs from import and excise duties, while public charging infrastructure had yet to keep pace with vehicle adoption.
"Today, EV adoption is mainly concentrated in urban areas. For long-distance travel, we're still a long way from where we need to be because we lack enough public chargers," he said after attending a media preview of the locally assembled Proton e.MAS 7 PHEV here.
Johari said EV adoption remains challenging for many Malaysians, particularly those living in flats and condominiums, as limited charging facilities and inadequate electrical capacity in older buildings make installing home chargers difficult.
"These are the issues we need to address. We are not against EVs. But we should not move ahead of the market before the ecosystem is ready. Ultimately, the problems faced by consumers will become problems for the government," he said.
He noted that the widespread adoption of internal combustion engine vehicles has been supported by Malaysia's network of about 3,500 petrol stations, providing an estimated 35,000 refuelling points nationwide.
"For EVs, the situation is very different. Even where public chargers are available, there may be only one or two, leaving motorists reluctant to travel long distances for fear they may be unable to recharge their vehicles.
"I asked China's trade minister how the country became so successful in promoting EVs. He told me it was because the government invested billions of dollars in public charging infrastructure.
"In Malaysia, however, we have spent billions on tax exemptions instead of investing in charging infrastructure. That is our challenge," he said.
Johari said Malaysia should emulate China's success by investing in EV charging infrastructure while exploring ways to generate revenue from growing EV adoption to fund further infrastructure development.
"We will also discuss with TNB how it can provide the substations needed to support more public chargers. These are matters that require careful planning.
"The government must look at the entire ecosystem. Otherwise, people will complain. Local authorities and the Housing and Local Government Ministry also need to plan ahead.
"In future public housing projects and flats, we need to determine whether space can be allocated for 10, 20 or even 30 public chargers, depending on the number of parking bays available," he said.
On the industrial front, Johari said foreign automakers investing in Malaysia must go beyond selling vehicles and contribute to the development of the country's automotive ecosystem.
He said investors should work alongside local entrepreneurs and component manufacturers to create jobs, strengthen domestic supply chains and generate broader economic benefits.
"They must coexist with the ecosystem that we already have and help build it together with our entrepreneurs and component manufacturers.
"The government also benefits. Today, Proton's tax contribution has reached RM806 million. This comes from corporate tax, excise duty, import duty and sales tax. All these taxes benefit the country.
"This is an industry that creates significant multiplier effects. But this can only happen if we adopt the mindset that investors coming into Malaysia must coexist with existing industries.
"We do not want investments that come here only to displace or undermine businesses that are already operating in the country," he said.
Johari cited Proton's partnership with China's Geely as an example of how foreign investment should strengthen local capabilities rather than simply use Malaysia as an export base.
"For example, Proton previously did not have the opportunity to enhance its production through advanced technologies.
"Geely possessed those technologies and shared them with Proton, with some intellectual property even being registered in Malaysia. This is what people call a true partnership, not one where a company simply comes here to export cars," he said.
He added that the national carmaker now employs about 9,700 workers and produces more than 150,000 vehicles annually, demonstrating how strategic partnerships can help develop domestic industrial capabilities.
Economist Dr Mohamad Idham Md Razak said attracting foreign automakers should go beyond providing market access and boosting vehicle sales, and instead be leveraged to strengthen domestic industrial capabilities.
He said without deeper linkages with local players, Malaysia risks remaining a consumption market rather than advancing further up the automotive value chain.
"Requiring contributions such as technology transfer, local sourcing, and collaboration with domestic firms helps generate spillover effects including skills development, productivity gains, and the growth of local suppliers.
"These are critical if Malaysia aims to strengthen its manufacturing base and remain competitive in the evolving automotive landscape, especially with the shift towards EVs and advanced mobility," he told Business Times.
Idham said Malaysia should prioritise high-impact contributions, including technology transfers in areas such as battery systems and smart manufacturing, while also fostering local vendor development, research and development investment and workforce upskilling.
He added that encouraging joint ventures and partnerships with local component manufacturers would further strengthen industrial linkages.
"That said, there is a balance to strike. If requirements are clear, consistent, and aligned with industry needs, they can actually enhance Malaysia's attractiveness by signalling a strong, long-term industrial policy and creating a more robust ecosystem for investors.
"However, if conditions are overly rigid or increase compliance costs significantly, they could discourage investment or divert it to competing countries," he said.
Idham said the key is to adopt a facilitative approach, where incentives and strategic partnerships encourage foreign automakers to deepen their investments, rather than imposing requirements that could discourage market entry.

Title: Reservoir Link eyes bigger role in liberalised gas market [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Reservoir Link Energy Bhd is positioning itself to capitalise on Malaysia's liberalised gas market after becoming one of the few listed companies to hold both a gas shipping licence and a liquefied natural gas (LNG) import licence, allowing it to participate across the gas value chain.
The oilfield services company joins a small group of Bursa Malaysia-listed firms, including Tenaga Nasional Bhd, Gas Malaysia Bhd, Uzma Bhd and Destini Bhd, whose subsidiaries hold both licences under the country's third party access (TPA) framework.
Reservoir Link executive director Thien Chiet Chai said the dual licences gave the company an edge over listed peers that only hold a gas shipping licence.
"A gas shipping licence enables the delivery of gas through the existing distribution network, which generally serves industrial customers.
"The LNG import licence goes further. It allows us to source LNG cargoes internationally and sell directly to large offtakers such as gas-fired power plants," he told Business Times.
He said the licences enable Reservoir Link to participate across the full gas value chain, from sourcing LNG overseas to delivering gas to end customers, rather than being confined to the midstream distribution segment.
The licences allow the company to supply gas to industrial customers under the TPA framework while creating longer-term opportunities through upcoming regasification terminal (RGT) infrastructure.
Thien said Reservoir Link is looking to leverage future RGT developments, including Petronas' planned terminal in Lumut and Gas Malaysia's proposed terminal in Yan, to supply gas directly to power producers.
"Strategically, these licences position Reservoir Link for the future of Malaysia's energy landscape," he said, adding that the gas business is expected to become a more meaningful earnings contributor as volumes scale.
The expansion comes as Malaysia experiences a surge in data centre investments, driving demand for reliable large-scale power generation.
"Data centre investment into Malaysia is driving demand for large baseload gas-fired power generation," Thien said.
He added that the gas business would complement Reservoir Link's existing well services and renewable energy businesses as the group broadens its energy portfolio.
However, he said securing LNG supply remains the biggest hurdle in commercialising the licences.
"Given the current global geopolitical environment, LNG allocations are tight and competition for cargoes is intense. Securing supply quotas will be the toughest hurdle in commercialising these licences," Thien said.
To overcome this, Reservoir Link is in discussions with international suppliers, including a Chinese government-linked corporation, to secure access to LNG quotas.
The company's strategy comes amid growing global demand for LNG as countries seek reliable energy sources while transitioning away from coal. Global LNG demand is projected to approach 700 million tonnes annually by 2050.
Malaysia remains a key LNG producer through Petronas' LNG complex in Bintulu, Sarawak, which has a production capacity of about 29.3 million tonnes per annum.
With Malaysia's gas market becoming increasingly liberalised and demand from industrial users and data centres continuing to rise, Reservoir Link believes its dual-licence position provides a strong platform for long-term growth.
"Liberalisation is opening the market to new entrants, and structural demand growth driven by industrial expansion and the data centre boom supports a constructive long-term view," Thien said.

Title: Lessons from Japan's debt burden
Article:
Japan today carries public debt exceeding 230 per cent of GDP—the highest among advanced economies. Yet for more than three decades, it largely escaped the debt crises, runaway inflation and surging borrowing costs that conventional economics would have predicted.
Government bond yields remained close to zero, inflation was virtually absent, and investors continued to regard Japanese Government Bonds (JGBs) as among the safest financial assets in the world.
It was one of the greatest macroeconomic anomalies of the modern era.
That anomaly is now beginning to fade.
The return of inflation after 2022 has fundamentally altered the environment that allowed Japan to sustain exceptionally high public debt at exceptionally low borrowing costs.
The country is not confronting an imminent sovereign debt crisis.
Rather, it is confronting something arguably more difficult: the gradual erosion of the economic conditions that made its unconventional fiscal and monetary model sustainable for over thirty years.
Japan Is Not Greece
Any discussion of Japan's debt must begin by recognising that Japan is fundamentally different from previous sovereign debt crises.
Unlike Greece during the Eurozone crisis, Japan borrows overwhelmingly in its own currency.
More than 90 per cent of Japanese Government Bonds are held domestically by households, banks, pension funds, insurance companies and, increasingly, the Bank of Japan itself.
Japan also remains the world's largest net international creditor, with overseas assets exceeding ¥500 trillion, providing a substantial external financial buffer.
These characteristics have allowed Japan to sustain debt levels that would almost certainly have triggered financial crises elsewhere.
Markets have remained confident not because Japan's debt is small—it is extraordinarily large—but because investors have confidence in Japan's institutions, monetary sovereignty and vast domestic savings.
The Bank of Japan's Extraordinary Intervention
Japan's current fiscal position cannot be understood without appreciating the unprecedented role played by the Bank of Japan (BOJ).
Following the collapse of Japan's asset-price bubble in the early 1990s, the economy entered decades of weak growth, stagnant wages and near-zero inflation.
Successive rounds of quantitative easing saw the BOJ purchase enormous quantities of government bonds to support economic activity and maintain exceptionally low borrowing costs.
Today, the BOJ owns roughly half of all outstanding Japanese Government Bonds, while its balance sheet has expanded to more than 100 per cent of GDP —an unprecedented scale among major advanced-economy central banks.
For many years, these extraordinary measures appeared remarkably successful.
Inflation remained close to zero, borrowing costs stayed negligible and the government continued financing large fiscal deficits without significant market disruption.
Inflation Has Changed the Rules
That environment changed dramatically following the global inflation shock beginning in 2022.
For much of the previous three decades, Japan experienced almost no inflation, interest rates remained close to zero and government debt-servicing costs were exceptionally low despite the country's enormous debt burden.
Those conditions allowed Japan to postpone difficult fiscal adjustments while maintaining financial stability.
Today, however, headline inflation has generally remained above the BOJ's long-standing 2 per cent target. Wage growth has accelerated, unionised workers have secured annual increases of around 5 per cent in recent years, and external shocks—including higher energy prices and geopolitical tensions—continue to exert upward pressure on prices.
At the same time, yields on Japanese Government Bonds have risen to levels not seen for many years. As older debt matures and must be refinanced at higher interest rates, the government's debt-servicing burden will inevitably increase.
The challenge therefore lies not simply in the size of Japan's debt, but in the interaction between an enormous debt stock and gradually rising borrowing costs.
The Yen's Decline Reflects Diverging Monetary Policies
The return of inflation has also transformed Japan's exchange-rate dynamics.
While the United States Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank responded aggressively by raising interest rates, the Bank of Japan proceeded with exceptional caution, only ending its negative interest-rate policy in 2024.
The widening interest-rate differential encouraged capital to flow into higher-yielding assets abroad.
The consequences have been striking. The Japanese yen has depreciated from around ¥103 per US dollar in early 2021 to approximately ¥160–163 per US dollar more recently—a depreciation of roughly 55 to 60 per cent.
Although a weaker yen benefits exporters and tourism, it also raises the cost of imported food, energy and industrial inputs, placing additional pressure on households and businesses.
The Impossible Triangle
Japan now confronts a policy dilemma that resembles an impossible triangle.
On the one hand, higher interest rates are needed to contain inflation and stabilise the yen. On the other, higher rates raise government borrowing costs at a time when public debt exceeds 230 per cent of GDP.
Meanwhile, renewed large-scale monetary easing to suppress bond yields would risk further weakening the currency and reigniting inflationary pressures.
The Bank of Japan therefore finds itself balancing three objectives that are increasingly difficult to achieve simultaneously: maintaining exceptionally low borrowing costs, preserving currency stability and containing inflation.
Managing one objective inevitably complicates the others.
This is not evidence of policy failure. Rather, it reflects the reality that the macroeconomic environment supporting Japan's policy framework has fundamentally changed.
The Demographic Headwind
Japan's fiscal challenge is ultimately driven by more than monetary policy alone.
Nearly 30 per cent of Japan's population is aged 65 or above, the highest proportion among major economies. The country's population has been shrinking since 2010, reducing labour-force growth while increasing expenditure on pensions, healthcare and long-term care.
An ageing society inevitably slows potential economic growth even as public spending rises.
Over time, this combination places increasing pressure on government finances regardless of the level of interest rates.
Monetary policy may alleviate these pressures temporarily, but it cannot reverse demographic realities.
A Lesson Beyond Japan
Despite increasingly difficult trade-offs, Japan remains unlikely to experience an acute sovereign debt crisis. Its deep domestic investor base, monetary sovereignty and extensive overseas assets provide important buffers that distinguish it from historical debt crises elsewhere.
Yet the broader significance of Japan's experience extends well beyond its own borders.
For much of the past two decades, exceptionally low global interest rates encouraged governments across advanced economies to accumulate unprecedented levels of public debt at relatively modest financing costs.
As inflation returns and monetary policy gradually normalises, those assumptions are being tested.
Japan may simply be the first advanced economy confronting this new reality—not because it borrowed the most, but because it reached the limits of unconventional monetary policy before anyone else.
The lesson is therefore not that Japan's debt crisis has finally arrived. Rather, it is that the extraordinary economic conditions which sustained exceptionally high public debt for more than three decades are steadily disappearing.
The challenge ahead is less about avoiding imminent default than about adapting fiscal and monetary policy to a world where inflation, higher interest rates and demographic change have fundamentally altered the rules of economic management.
That may prove to be the more enduring test—not only for Japan, but eventually for many advanced economies.

Title: Uniting people through football
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Mosque communities, young footballers and Malaysians from diverse backgrounds will come together for the inaugural Federal Territory Islamic Religious Council's (MAIWP) 2026 Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Religious Affairs) Football Championship Cup next month.
The invitational nine-a-side tournament, themed "Aksi Bola Merdeka", will take place in Bangi on Aug 29-30, which is also the Merdeka Month.
Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Religious Affairs) Dr Zulkifli Hasan said the championship aimed to promote unity, patriotism, brotherhood and healthy living while strengthening the role of mosques within local communities.
Organised under the Semarak Masjid Bersama Belia initiative, the programme seeks to position mosques as dynamic hubs for sports, recreational and community activities alongside their religious and spiritual functions.
"We want to see mosques not only as places that unite Muslims, but also as institutions that celebrate differences and encourage respect for others," he told a press conference after announcing the championship at Masjid At-Taqwa, Taman Tun Dr Ismail.
Also present were MAIWP chairman Datuk Syed Kamarulzaman Syed Kabeer and MAIWP chief executive officer Datuk Mohd Nizam Yahya.
The tournament will feature 32 teams representing various mosques nationwide, with each state Islamic religious department sending two teams, and 10 teams representing mosques in the federal territories.
Each squad will comprise six employees from the state Islamic religious department or council, seven players aged 18 years and below, and at least two non-Muslims, reflecting the organisers' emphasis on inclusion and social harmony.
Former national footballers Abdul Malik Abdul Rahman, Muhammad Hardi Jaafar and Indra Putra Mahyuddin have been appointed championship ambassadors.
The champions will receive RM3,000, a trophy and medals, while the runners-up will take home RM2,000 and medals. The two joint third-placed teams will receive RM1,000 each.
Zulkifli said the championship was inspired by the success of an earlier futsal league involving mosques in the federal territories, which received an encouraging response from youths.
He said sports provided an effective avenue to draw young people closer to mosques while exposing them to community, religious and character-building programmes.
"When there is a football programme, there will also be congregational prayers. From there, we can encourage them to participate in other activities.
"Most importantly, they will be in a positive environment close to mosques," he said.
Indra Putra welcomed the initiative, describing it as a positive platform to get more young people involved in mosque programmes.
"This is a good programme. It encourages young players to participate in activities organised by the religious councils and, most importantly, encourages them to become involved with the mosque," he said.

Title: Alphabet rolls back AI image generation in Google Earth over policy violations
Article:
MEXICO CITY: Alphabet's Google said on Friday it was rolling back an AI image-generation feature it had introduced in Google Earth just a day earlier, after users shared images that appeared to violate the company's policies.
The feature, powered by Google's Nano Banana 2 AI model, had allowed users to generate photorealistic images based on Google Earth's satellite, aerial and 3D imagery by typing a text prompt for any location around the globe.
The tool had come under criticism over its potential for misinformation, as it allowed users to create fake scenarios on top of real imagery of monuments and landmarks.
"We've seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we've also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies," Google said on X, adding that it was pausing the capability while it worked on stronger guardrails.
Google did not specify what types of images violated its policies. It said the images did not appear in the main Google Earth experience and were watermarked as AI-generated.
While tech giants have rushed to integrate AI tools across their products, they have had to adjust, restrict or temporarily disable features in response to user violations, misinformation and policy concerns.
Meta earlier this month discontinued Muse Image, an AI feature that allowed users to generate images using public Instagram accounts, after drawing widespread criticism over privacy concerns, including from a Hollywood union.

Title: Fire breaks out at Red Square church in Moscow
Article:
MOSCCOW: A fire broke out early Saturday at the St Basil's Cathedral in Moscow but was contained, TASS news agency said, quoting operational services.
"On the first floor, in the director's office, personal belongings and furniture caught fire. The area of the fire was around 10 sq. metres.
Around 10 fire engines were deployed to the scene. The fire is currently contained," the agency's source said.

Title: Cubs spotted in Malaysia's first tiger reserve but poaching remains key threat
Article:
JERANTUT:  Despite encouraging signs that Malayan tigers are breeding in the country's first dedicated tiger reserve, conservationists say poaching and prey depletion remain the biggest threats to the species' long-term survival.
Camera traps at the Al-Sultan Abdullah Royal Tiger Reserve (ASARTR) in Ulu Tembeling have recorded Malayan tiger cubs and juveniles, providing the strongest evidence yet that the critically endangered species is breeding in the protected area.
Captured through scientific monitoring, the images have raised hopes the reserve provides the conditions needed not only for tigers to survive but also to reproduce.
While it is still too early to determine the tiger population within the reserve, conservationists have established a baseline that will allow them to monitor whether efforts to protect and grow the Malayan tiger population are succeeding over time.
The Habitat Foundation programme director Dr Ahmad Zafir Abdul Wahab said poaching and prey depletion remained the greatest threats to the reserve's tiger population.
To counter them, he said Panthera Malaysia and the Pahang State Parks Corporation (PTNP) maintained a constant deployment of rangers conducting deep-forest patrols and enforcement operations.
He said the camera trap surveys had also enabled conservationists to establish a scientific baseline for the tiger population, providing a benchmark to assess whether protection measures were safeguarding the species and increasing its numbers. He added that ensuring an adequate food supply was equally critical.
To address prey depletion, conservationists had established pastures to increase populations of key prey species, including sambar deer and barking deer.
As deer and other prey populations recover, tigers are more likely to remain within their core range, reducing the need to venture beyond in search of food, where they face greater risks from poaching and other human-related threats.
[[nid:1501712]]
The conservation measures form part of a broader effort to ensure ASARTR's long-term viability as one of the country's last strongholds for the Malayan tiger.
Gazetted on Aug 31, 2023, ASARTR was established by the Pahang government through PTNP to strengthen protection for the Malayan tiger and its habitat while conserving the wider forest ecosystem.
The reserve spans 134,183 hectares in two phases. Phase One covers 92,649ha, comprising the Gunung Aais Forest Reserve and its additional reserve, while Phase Two covers 41,533ha in the Tekai-Tembeling Forest Reserve.
Linked to Taman Negara, the protected landscape now extends over 568,500ha, making it one of Malaysia's largest.
Sultan of Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah Ri'ayatuddin Al-Mustafa Billah Shah declared the reserve on July 29, 2023, underscoring the state's commitment to wildlife conservation.
Global Tiger Day is observed annually on July 29 to raise awareness of the threats facing wild tiger populations.
PTNP chief executive officer Zainal Abidin Othman said camera trap monitoring indicated the tiger population within the reserve remained healthy and was consistent with the forest's carrying capacity.
He said the reserve was established to expand the tiger's roaming range, strengthen habitat protection and support joint conservation of the forest ecosystem.
ASARTR is managed through a public-private partnership involving PTNP, the Pahang Forestry Department and Enggang Management Services (EMS).
EMS works with conservation organisations, including Bringing Back Our Rare Animals (Bora), Nature Based Solutions Malaysia, The Habitat Foundation and Panthera Malaysia, on initiatives covering habitat and prey management, scientific research, monitoring, enforcement, patrolling and community engagement.
Panthera Malaysia country director Wai Yee Lam said camera trap surveys conducted since 2023 had recorded encouraging evidence, including the presence of juveniles and cubs.
She said camera traps, together with regular ranger patrols, enabled researchers to better understand tiger distribution, habitat use and population trends while strengthening protection on the ground.
[[nid:1501711]]
Community participation also forms an important part of conservation efforts.
Under Panthera Malaysia's Community Ranger Programme, Orang Asli villagers have been trained as rangers to patrol the reserve, deter illegal activities and protect wildlife.
Nature Based Solutions Malaysia project development lead Dr Julia Ng said the Orang Asli's deep knowledge of the forest made them well placed to help safeguard the landscape for future generations.
Dr Ahmad Zafir said the reserve protected one of Peninsular Malaysia's remaining lowland forest ecosystems, a preferred habitat for tigers and other large mammals.
He said conserving the Malayan tiger was essential to maintaining healthy forests because, as an apex predator, it regulated prey species such as deer and wild boar, helping to keep ecosystems in balance.
Beyond anti-poaching operations, conservation efforts at ASARTR include prey augmentation, pasture and nursery development, habitat management, research, monitoring, patrolling, enforcement and community engagement.
The reserve also provides refuge for other threatened species, including the
seladang
, Malayan tapir and Asian elephant.
EMS Decision Support Services lead William Yap said about 90 personnel were based in Jerantut to support operations within and around the reserve, including some 65 frontline patrollers.

Title: Kidnapper of US TV host's mother apologised for her death
Article:
LOS ANGELES: The alleged kidnapper of a US television star's mother apologised as he told her family six days after her disappearance that she had died, according to a note released by police.
Nancy Guthrie, 84, vanished from her home in Arizona on the night of Jan 31-Feb 1, and her body has never been found.
Her daughter Savannah Guthrie, the popular anchor of a major morning news programme, has repeatedly brought the case before the public, pleading for help.
In a statement on Friday, six months after the kidnapping, the Pima County Sheriff's Department said the search for Guthrie was ongoing and asked for public assistance as it released two purported ransom notes sent to a local television station on Feb 2 and Feb 6.
The first demanded millions of dollars in Bitcoin for Guthrie's safe return and threatened to kill her if her family did not comply.
The second informed the family that "she perished shortly after she was taken" and "is buried in nature now".
The writer implied that Guthrie died of natural causes, taking her captors by surprise.
"We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition... We believe it was heart related," it said.
"We are truly sorry," the note added, claiming that "we never intended to hurt her".
The content of the notes was reported by US media in June, prompting another plea from her daughter for information on her mother's whereabouts.
"Please do the right thing for us, for our family, for our children, and we love our mom, and we'll never stop looking for her, never," she said.
The kidnapping in Tucson, Arizona, made headlines across the United States.
Interest intensified when security camera footage released by authorities showed a masked, apparently armed man at the house, which lies in the desert suburbs of the city.
US President Donald Trump said he had been following the case.
"I hope they find her," he told reporters. "That family has gone through hell."
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Explosions in Kyiv, mayor says city 'under ballistic missile attack'
Article:
KYIV, (Ukraine): Explosions were heard in Kyiv earlier today as the city's mayor said the Ukrainian capital was being attacked by ballistic missiles.
"Explosions in the city. Kyiv is under ballistic missile attack. Stay in shelters!" Vitali Klitschko said. An AFP journalist also reported hearing explosions.
More than 10 explosions were heard in a row, AFP journalists reported, adding that the intensity of the blasts triggered car alarms on the streets.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump earlier this week for talks that came as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes after US-led diplomatic efforts to end the war stalled.
Zelenskyy said following the meeting that Trump had agreed to license the production of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, but the US president only said that "many things were discussed" and "the meeting went very well!" — AFP

Title: Negri Sembilan voters head to the polls today
Article:
SEREMBAN: Voters in Negri Sembilan will fulfil their democratic rights and civic duty today in the 16th state election (PRN) to elect their new representatives.
A total of 859,760 registered voters, including 7,391 postal voters, will determine which coalition will be given the mandate to govern Negri Sembilan following a 14-day campaign period that ended at midnight.
Voting will begin simultaneously at 8am at 401 polling centres across the state involving 1,668 streams before closing at 6pm.
The Election Commission (EC) is targeting a voter turnout of between 72 and 75 per cent today. Results are expected as early as 10pm, with the full outcome anticipated before midnight.
Last Tuesday's early voting recorded a turnout of 91.06 per cent, with 14,995 military and police personnel and their spouses casting their ballots.
Meanwhile, the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) forecasts clear weather across most parts of Negri Sembilan, including Seremban, Jempol, Jelebu, Kuala Pilah, Tampin, Port Dickson and Rembau, throughout the morning and until noon. Heavy rain and thunderstorms are expected in most districts in the afternoon.
A total of 36 state legislative assembly (DUN) seats are being contested in the election, involving 103 candidates.
Pakatan Harapan (PH) is contesting all 36 seats, followed by Barisan Nasional (BN) with 25 candidates, Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) with 24 candidates and Perikatan Nasional (PN) with 11 candidates.
Other parties contesting are Berjasa, Parti Orang Asli Malaysia (ASLI) and the Socialist Party of Malaysia (PSM), each fielding one candidate, alongside four independents.
The election features 22 three-cornered contests, 11 straight fights, two four-cornered contests and one five-cornered contest.
In the 2023 Negri Sembilan state election, PH won 17 of the 36 seats, followed by BN with 14 and PN with five. The Negri Sembilan State Legislative Assembly was dissolved on June 5.
For the latest news on the 16th Negri Sembilan state election, visit [https://prn.bernama.com/n9](https://prn.bernama.com/n9).

Title: Lebanon president says Israeli blasts near castle 'direct threat' to recent deal
Article:
BEIRUT: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun on Friday warned that Israeli detonations near a Unesco-listed castle threatened a recent deal with Israel, which in turn said it had razed Hizbollah tunnels there.
Lebanon's National News Agency (NNA) reported that "Israeli forces triggered very powerful explosions" overnight, specifically "in the area of the Beaufort fortress", a Crusader-era castle located near the southern border occupied by Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army had destroyed "terror tunnels in the Beaufort area" using approximately 700 tonnes of explosives.
Aoun labelled it "an extremely dangerous escalation" and "a direct threat to the process which was launched as part of the framework agreement" reached with Israel during US-sponsored talks last month, his office said.
Under the Israel-Lebanon deal, Lebanon's army is to disarm Hizbollah and the Israeli military is to withdraw from "pilot zones", where Lebanese forces will subsequently deploy.
The timing of the blasts ahead of another round of talks with Israel in Rome next week "sends negative messages and undermines international efforts aimed at consolidating stability", Aoun added.
The NNA said huge blasts resounded over a large area, shattering glass in nearby villages, while an AFP correspondent heard large explosions and saw dust covering a swathe of forest.
Citing Lebanon's National Centre for Geophysics, Aoun's statement said the detonations "created ground waves equivalent to a 3.8-magnitude earthquake on the Richter scale".
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam condemned "the ongoing Israeli aggressions in the south", including "the damage to archaeological sites... that constitute a precious part of the history of our homeland".
UNDER OCCUPATION
Beaufort Castle was added last week to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger.
Lebanon's culture ministry said the explosions struck "the area opposite the fortress", warning that "the vibrations from the explosions may have caused damage" in the castle's vicinity.
It said technical teams were unable to conduct an on-the-ground assessment because "the site is under occupation".
The Israeli army said "the tunnel network served as a central command centre" for Hizbollah and consisted of "several underground levels that were built over the course of two decades".
Netanyahu and Katz said the explosions followed a "blatant violation of the ceasefire agreement" by Hizbollah, which Israel's army accused on Wednesday of launching an explosive drone at a military vehicle.
Lebanese parliament speaker Nabih Berri, a Hizbollah ally, condemned the detonations, while the Iran-backed group urged Lebanese authorities to act "at all political and diplomatic levels to stop the destructive crimes being carried out by the enemy".
Hizbollah has not claimed any attacks since a ceasefire with Israel came into force on June 20 after a US-Iran memorandum of understanding on ending the broader Middle East war.
While violence has declined since then, Lebanon continues to report Israeli strikes and artillery shelling in the south, as well as detonations of buildings in southern villages.
The NNA reported three "violent" explosions on Friday evening on the outskirts of Taybeh.
Iran-backed Hizbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war on March 2 with attacks on Israel.
Israel retaliated with a massive bombing campaign and a ground offensive that Lebanese authorities say have killed more than 4,300 people.
Israel's army continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon extending about 10 kilometres (six miles) into Lebanese territory along the border.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Negri Sembilan decides: Voters hold key to state's political future [WATCH]
Article:
SEREMBAN:   The  political direction of Negri Sembilan hangs in the balance today as more than 850,000 eligible voters cast their ballots in a closely watched state election.
The battle for the 36-seat state assembly, marked by two weeks of intense campaigning, not only allowed voters to raise issues close to their hearts for the next state government to address, but also once again tested the ties between Pakatan Harapan and Barisan Nasional, which are partners in the federal administration but political rivals in Negri Sembilan.
Similar to the recent Johor polls, PH and BN are contesting against each other, with tensions in the state between the two coalitions  intensifying after all 14 BN assemblymen withdrew their support for PH's Datuk Seri Aminuddin Harun as menteri besar in April.
However, unlike the Johor election, PH entered the contest as the caretaker state government, banking on its two-term record in administering Negri Sembilan and Aminuddin's track record as leader.
Pushing a message of continuity and stability for Negri Sembilan, PH is contesting all seats with a target of increasing its seat tally to 22 in this election, five more than the 17 seats the coalition won in the 2023 state election.
This ambition is reflected, among others, through Aminuddin's risky decision to vacate his Sikamat seat and contest in Linggi, a constituency considered a BN stronghold, in a bid to expand PH's representation in the state assembly.
[[nid:1501678]]
While cooperation between BN and Perikatan Nasional during the Johor election was seen as a one-sided affair, the two coalitions, which are rivals at the federal level, enter the Negri Sembilan polls  with an electoral understanding in the hope that a transfer of votes between their supporters could take place and help swing Malay votes in their favour.
BN is contesting 25 seats, with the rest contested by PN, in the hope of winning support from the Malay electorate, who political observers say account for 70 per cent of total voters.
The electoral understanding between the two coalitions seemed convincing at first, but showed flaws during the campaign period, when there was a noticeable lack of communication and coordination on several issues.
One of them involved remarks made by PN election director Datuk Seri Muhammad Sanusi Md Nor, which drew flak not only from the public and political rivals, but also from BN leaders, including its chairman, Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
Zahid's public rebuke of Sanusi, who is also  Kedah menteri besar, urging him to focus on his own state, reinforced the perception among political observers that BN remains cautious about committing to a broader and more formal alliance with PN beyond Negri Sembilan.
Political analyst Professor James Chin, however, believes that BN, through its electoral understanding with PN, is likely to sweep most of the Malay-majority constituencies.
"At the grassroots level, the Umno machinery is working well with the moon (Pas) machinery. So well, in fact, that I think the majority of Malay seats will go to Umno, with a few going to Pas," said Chin, a professor at the University of Tasmania's Asia Institute, in a Facebook post.
Another issue that took centre stage during the final week of campaigning was the Royal Commission of Inquiry report on Tabung Haji, which not only
triggered an exchange of statements between party leaders, but also sparked widespread debate among the public, particularly on social media.
While some observers said the issue was likely to affect or dent the electoral prospects of parties linked to the report, others have argued otherwise, noting that the majority of social media users were from the younger generation.
According to a survey by the Ilham Centre, the average composition of young voters in Negri Sembilan stands at around 48 per cent, while 15 of the 36 state constituencies have a young voter composition exceeding 50 per cent.
The five constituencies with the highest proportion of young voters are Bagan Pinang (60 per cent), Paroi (59 per cent), Gemas (58 per cent), Serting (58 per cent) and Labu (55 per cent).
'This means that almost every election outcome is now directly influenced by the preferences of the younger generation," it said in its latest analysis on the state election.
"The determination of their political stance is no longer based primarily on candidate personalities, but is increasingly guided by party branding and major narratives circulating in the social media space."
Political analyst Dr Azmi Hassan said a PH victory, whether by a simple majority or a landslide, would demonstrate that Negri Sembilan voters not only continued to support PH at the state level, but also wanted Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim to continue leading the federal government.
"Not only will it provide momentum heading into the next state election, which will most likely be in  Melaka, but it will also ease
the pressure on Anwar to dissolve Parliament and call  the next general election," he said.
Azmi also said a BN-PN victory would suggest that the cooperation between the two coalitions had passed its "proof of concept" and gained  acceptance among voters.
"I believe successful BN-PN cooperation in Negri Sembilan will likely carry over into future state elections, particularly Melaka.
"On the other hand, if the BN-PN alliance fails to secure a majority, it would suggest that this working relationship is effective only in states where Umno is traditionally dominant, such as Johor and perhaps Melaka.
"In states where BN is not as strong and does not enjoy majority influence, the cooperation may not work because PN supporters may not fully transfer their votes to BN candidates," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Trump threatens to hit Iran 'very hard'
Article:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump threatened on Friday to hit Iran "very hard", as US media reported he was considering renewed heavy attacks as soon as this weekend, including against energy infrastructure targets.
After more than five months of war, which began on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, there appears to be no end to the conflict, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming.
"We'll be hitting him very hard and, you know, at some point they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore'," Trump said on Friday as he hosted a cabinet meeting at the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland.
*The Wall Street Journal* later reported that Trump had ordered a fresh attack aimed at convincing Teheran to surrender, which could begin as soon as this weekend, citing unnamed US officials.
CBS News, meanwhile, reported that the United States and Israel were planning joint strikes on energy-related targets, possibly throughout the weekend. Such targets would likely include oil refineries and power plants.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Iran's vital infrastructure throughout the war, vowing last week to destroy a bridge or power plant every time ships in the vital Strait of Hormuz are attacked.
The president had not yet given the green light for the campaign, but Israel and the US were coordinating, CBS said, citing multiple unnamed sources.
The report comes just days after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Washington and met Trump and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Some White House aides voiced strong objections to the plan during the cabinet meeting, the CBS report said.
If the plan went ahead, it would mark the first time Israel has joined attacks on Iran since the initial phase of the war.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Hundreds rally in Madrid against migrant 'invasion' in Ceuta
Article:
MADRID: Hundreds of anti-migrant protesters rallied outside Morocco's embassy in Madrid on Friday evening to denounce what they called a migrant "invasion" of Spain's north African enclave of Ceuta.
Several protesters performed Nazi salutes, some openly and without covering their faces.
Local authorities in Ceuta said around 60,000 migrants had entered the enclave in recent days, although the Spanish government said Friday evening that "practically the entirety" of those who crossed had already returned to Morocco.
"Spain, Christian and not Muslim!" and "National unity!" protesters chanted, many dressed entirely in black, an AFP journalist said.
[[nid:1501743]]
Some demonstrators carried a large banner reading "Remigration" – a term promoted by several far-right groups in Europe that refers to the forced or encouraged return of migrants or people of immigrant background.
Others waved Spain's red-and-yellow flags and called for the defence of "Spanish identity."
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialist government, which has defended a relatively open approach to migration compared with many other European countries, was also targeted by demonstrators.
Protesters accused him of "selling" Spain "to Muslims" and blamed him for what they described as an "out-of-control crisis."
A heavy police presence was deployed around the  embassy, including a helicopter and a surveillance drone overhead.

Title: US ICE detains Johns Hopkins researcher as airport arrests surge
Article:
WASHINGTON: US immigration agents arrested a Johns Hopkins University researcher at an airport where she planned to board a domestic flight as immigration arrests by President Donald Trump's administration have surged at airports in recent weeks.
Here are more details:
Lawyers say there has been an uptick in immigration enforcement and arrests at airports.
They say the focus has been on those who have overstayed visas, even if they have pending applications for asylum or marriage.
The number of people who overstay temporary US visas annually is in the hundreds of thousands, government data shows.
Fatima Ameaka, who is from Cameroon and an employee at the Bloomberg School of Public Health, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at the Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said on Friday.
DHS said she had overstayed her visa, which allowed her to stay until June 2024, and would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.
Johns Hopkins said Ameaka was "a respected member" of its community and the school was arranging support for her.
US media, including *The New York Times*, reported this week that foreign citizens with expired visas are being arrested as they travel through airports in an expansion of an arrangement between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration (TSA).
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Figures behind rush for Hormuz oil export alternatives
Article:
LONDON: Disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has prompted oil-producing countries in the Gulf to accelerate plans for alternative export routes, with a series of pipeline projects announced or revived.
Here is a breakdown of the proposals.
REGIONAL PICTURE
A total of 14.95 million barrels per day (mbd) of crude oil was exported through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Iran exported around 1.69 mbd and is expected to continue relying on Hormuz over the long term given its effective control of the waterway, Andrew Wilson of BRS Shipbrokers told AFP.
"Iran is just going to produce as much as it can, ship as much to China as it can. It's not really such an issue," he said.
Of the remaining 13.26 mbd, as much as 11.5 mbd could eventually be rerouted by maximising existing pipeline capacity and completing planned projects, according to official announcements and industry experts.
SAUDI ARABIA
Before the war broke out in late February, Saudi Arabia transported around 2 mbd of crude through its East-West Pipeline linking Abqaiq, near the Gulf coast, with the Red Sea port of Yanbu, according to the IEA.
State oil giant Aramco said in March 2025 it had increased the pipeline's capacity to 7 mbd, leaving up to 5 mbd of spare capacity.
Riyadh is also planning a further expansion of up to 2 mbd, according to the US-based Institute for Energy Research (IER).
[[nid:1501656]]
The IER said it was "unclear" whether this would involve upgrades to the existing line or construction of a parallel pipeline.
The project could potentially be completed by 2030/2031, Wilson told AFP.
UNITED ARAB EMIRATES
Before the conflict, the UAE exported around 1.1 mbd of crude through its Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP), which links inland oil fields with the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
The IEA said the pipeline had a capacity of 1.8 mbd, leaving an additional 0.7 mbd available.
The UAE said in May it was fast-tracking construction of a second pipeline that would run parallel to the existing route before extending to the country's northern coast, allowing crude produced north of Hormuz to bypass the strait.
The project would double export capacity through Fujairah and is expected to enter service next year, according to the Abu Dhabi Media Office.
IRAQ
The US State Department said earlier in July that plans were under way to restore a major pipeline linking Iraq's oil fields with Syria's Mediterranean coast.
Washington is overseeing an international consortium "to execute the technical and financial aspects of this project", which is expected to have an initial capacity of 2 mbd, the department said.
No timetable has been announced. However, political and investment hurdles risk delaying the project, Wilson warned.
KUWAIT AND BAHRAIN
Neither Kuwait nor Bahrain currently has a pipeline route that bypasses Hormuz.
However, both have recently held discussions with Saudi Arabia on a possible connection to its pipeline network, according to the IER.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: At Farnborough airshow, tech and geopolitics drive aviation innovation
Article:
ON  the first day of the Farnborough airshow last week, an unusual-looking craft with upward-pointing propellers along its wings rose into the sky from the main runway: the new electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) lightweight "air taxi" from Britain's Vertical Aerospace.
The Farnborough show and accompanying military and civilian aviation trade event have long showcased a mix of breakthroughs, breathlessly announced sales of existing aircraft types and a look into the future.
This year, however, there was a greater sense of urgency and an increasingly dramatic pace of change, fuelled by new developments in materials and power storage, chips and artificial intelligence  alongside deteriorating geopolitical relations.
Vertical Aerospace's first public take-off flight of its "air taxi" is a case in point. Without huge leaps forward in battery power, electric motors and other airframe elements, it would be unable to get airborne — let alone achieve its claimed 160km-plus flying range.
Demand for new aircraft has rebounded from a dip during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020.
"Defence was about 30 per cent of our business only a few years back and now it's more than 50 per cent," said Matthew Pritchard, vice-president for sales and customer engagement at Ontic, which supplies equipment to major aviation manufacturers as well as maintenance and repair services.
The result brings several paradoxes: major aviation manufacturers, particularly Boeing and Airbus, now have multiple years of orders for airliner types dating back several decades.
Older jet fighters such as the 1990s-era Eurofighter and Lockheed Martin F-16 are also seeing ongoing and often rising sales on the back of growing tensions.
Simultaneously, other new technology is leaping forward. Dutch company Robin Radar Systems — which started out building small airport radars to detect flocks of birds but has since moved into anti-drone technology — was just one of several that told this columnist that their firms were undergoing very rapid growth.
In total, Farnborough recorded almost US$85 billion in deals, both military and civilian.
"We are literally learning in real time," said former RAF Typhoon jet fighter pilot Andrew Hawkes, now leading the European rollout of defence tech firm Shield AI's stealth vertical take-off X Bat drone, describing the "evolving threat environment" as a key driver of developments.
Shield AI, founded in 2015 by former US Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, is already operating its non-stealth V-Bat in Ukraine and other combat zones.
The company says the new X-Bat will fly for the first time before the end of the year under the control of an autonomous AI pilot and, when operational, will carry the same weapons as a much more expensive US-made piloted F-35 for a fraction of the cost.
Some of the largest announcements at Farnborough this year relate to the Anglo-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Programme, intended to deliver a new "sixth-generation" stealth fighter into service by 2035.
The wars in Ukraine and now the Gulf have supercharged demand for new military tech.
Design processes increasingly take advantage of lessons from Ukraine, where engineers say they face a constant battle to stay ahead of new forms of Russian jamming, including against Elon Musk's Starlink system that had been key to the operation of multiple drone types.
At Farnborough, fast-growing autonomous weapons maker Anduril unveiled a new autonomous twin-rotor vertical take-off Thunder drone, designed to operate at low altitude over a highly contested battlefield and both replace and augment existing high-tech attack helicopters alongside other cheaper drones.
"Manufacturing technology has come pretty far in the composite space, led by Formula One and other aerospace folks," said Phil Kelly, senior vice-president for business development and a former British jet pilot. "That allows us to build lighter, stronger."
While few if any of the aircraft on display at Farnborough this year have been predominantly designed through AI, engineers there said AI processes could considerably speed both computer model testing and regulatory processes.
For now, more traditional aircraft are still selling well. Airbus and Boeing between them received more than 1,200 combined orders for commercial aircraft in the first half of the year.
Whether that civilian boom can survive rising energy prices and disruption from international tensions is another question.
Either way, the world is headed fast into uncharted waters and that will bring the global aviation sector — like the rest of us — as much risk as opportunity.
The writer is from Reuters
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Preserve uniqueness of Kuching's old quarter
Article:
THE uniqueness of Kuching and what makes it a marvel for visitors is that the city is replete with old buildings,  put up mostly during the era of the Brooke Raj from the 1840s to the 1940s.
The Old Court House right in the centre of the city has been transformed into a sprawling warren of restaurants interspersed with a garden courtyard and some Brooke memorabilia, making it a lively and popular oasis amidst the city hustle and bustle.
A stone's throw away is the General Post Office, easily the most impressive of the city's old buildings with a colonnade of Corinthian columns spanning an entire city block.
The new era of emails and social media has meant postal services — like almost everywhere in the world — have lost their popularity.
This has put paid to the utility of this handsome old building, now a pale shadow of its heyday when it was a hive of human activity.
There has been talk for some time of preserving the building and turning it into one more functional place befitting its enduring grandeur. But what might that be?
Now Premier Tan Sri Abang Johari Openg may be on to something. Speaking at the opening of another building transformed into a high-end hotel and elderly-care centre in Kuching this week, he pointed to another old post office building in Singapore which is  now the Fullerton Hotel.
The only problem is that the two-storey General Post Office  building in Kuching is hemmed in with little space  for an  annex, unless the state government acquires the rows of shophouses behind the building.
But unless those shophouses are also preserved and somehow integrated into the General Post Office building, Carpenter Street — where the shophouses sit — may lose the charm and character that make the  old quarter of Kuching so distinctively attractive.
It will do well for the state government — once it has successfully acquired the General Post Office building from the federal government — to consult architects and town planners and maybe request for proposals on how best to go about this preservation undertaking.
The state may, of course, opt for a preservation and transformation scope limited to just the General Post Office building or be more ambitious and try to blend the restoration into the building's immediate vicinity.
Unlike in Singapore or George Town where much work has gone into not just preserving old shophouses but also transforming them into more upscale and therefore more valuable uses, Kuching has so far not seriously tried this restoration route.
Since shophouses are mostly privately owned, unless  legislation with strict rules and guidelines on preservation are introduced and coupled with perhaps some incentives, most of Kuching's old shophouses are likely to remain in their current somewhat dilapidated state.
The likely restoration and transformation of the General Post Office building and the  shophouses nearest to it may be considered as a test-bed for  similar future exercises,  which will gradually upgrade, enhance and modernise Kuching's heritage-laden pre-cincts without destroying their time-worn character.
Kuching's old city centre is its unique selling proposition and much thought and careful work must go into its essential preservation and restoration.
The writer views developments in the nation, region and the wider world from his vantage point in Kuching
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Felda task force report to be released in coming months, says Anwar
Article:
JEMPOL: The special task force report on the Federal Land Development Authority (Felda) is expected to be completed within the next few months, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.
He said the report would be made public once it was finalised, in line with the government's commitment to transparency.
Anwar also urged the public to read the report, just as they had been encouraged to examine the findings of the Royal Commission of Inquiry (RCI) into Lembaga Tabung Haji.
"We have already released the Tabung Haji report. In a few months, when the Felda task force report is completed, we will release that as well.
"Read the Felda report," he said during his speech at the Grand Finale Kekal Harapan programme in Jeram Padang tonight.
He said the government was committed to correcting mistakes of the past as part of its responsibility to the people.
Anwar, who is also the finance minister, said the federal and state governments should work together to ensure the smoother implementation of policies and programmes, particularly those aimed at safeguarding the welfare of the people.

Title: NST Leader: Bumpy ride looms as telcos ride 5G wave
Article:
FOR Malaysians, high-speed home broadband and 5G mobile subscriptions are either considered  a divine right or a commodity. Subscriptions are affordable, especially prepaid, that go for as low as RM35 a month with unlimited data.
That makes Malaysia's Internet and 5G penetration ubiquitous. Practically everyone owns a smartphone. That has pushed overall Internet usage to 98.3 per cent for a population of 35 million. Household access to fixed high-speed broadband is at 97.1 per cent, or 50 subscriptions per 100 premises, covering 5.04 million homes and businesses.
Mobile high-speed broadband topped 130.7 subscriptions per 100 inhabitants or 45 million accounts. In just over 30 years, Malaysians have adapted with stunning alacrity to the Internet, high-speed broadband and 5G mobile subscriptions, thanks to government-backed infrastructure policies.
Populated area coverage has reached almost 100 per cent under the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission's (MCMC) Jendela digital architecture roadmap.
More than 9.03 million premises are plugged into fibreoptic networks, clocking an average baseline speed of 101.5 Mbps across all Internet service providers.
Eighty per cent of Malaysians maintain at least two active digital subscriptions, such as video and music streaming, food delivery and e-hailing, spending RM80 to RM120 monthly.
Nevertheless, the peeves users confront daily are dropped signals, 5G dropping to 4G and transmission blind spots at highway stretches.
The MCMC, anticipating demand for better access, plans to build 77 telecommunications towers on 50km of highway stretches nationwide that have poor mobile coverage, part of the government's commitment to developing smart highways.
The zeal to build these digital link-ups to expand reach and jack up speed is driven by competition, ever-changing consumer habits and infrastructure upgrades.
It's also driven by content creators and aggregators clamouring for semi-urban and rural users now that urban markets have saturated.
To be profitable, investments in content demand massive users, which translates into bigger advertisers and lower-tier, ad-supported subscription plans.
That's why Malaysian telcos offer deals with free smartphones and  streaming services to thwart mobile and broadband users from switching to the next  competitor.
Motivated by maintaining customer loyalty, competition among telcos is great for consumers for now, but price wars can be destructive to the point of worsening network quality.
If profitability is clobbered, telcos lose capital expenditure to maintain towers, expand rural 5G coverage and fix blind spots.
What happens then during hyper competition? It compels major mergers, like Celcom and Digi, whose consolidation propped up profits but shrunk the market pool. Over time, the same scenario repeats itself and eventually, there will be lesser competitive telcos.
